summary: Describes OSPF-OR, extensions to OSPF for mobile ad hoc networks. They include link-local signaling, an OSPF-MANET interface, smaller incremental Hello packets, optimized flooding and fewer adjacencies. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF-OR adapts OSPFv3 for wireless networks whose links can change as devices move. It reduces repeated neighbor information, limits which routers relay updates, and can avoid some unnecessary adjacencies.

questions: ospf for mobile ad hoc networks
what are overlapping relays in ospf
subtitle: OSPF changes for mobile ad hoc networks, with smaller updates and selective relaying.

tldr.problem: OSPF's usual interface and update behavior assumes links that are more stable than wireless links in a mobile ad hoc network.
tldr.mechanism: OSPF-OR adds a MANET interface, incremental Hello messages, optimized flooding through overlapping relays, and a method for reducing unnecessary adjacencies.
tldr.outcome: The extensions are Experimental, not an Internet Standards Track specification. RFC 5820 is updated by RFC 7137.

today: RFC 5820 is an Experimental specification, not an Internet Standards Track specification, and is updated by RFC 7137. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why OSPF Needs MANET Extensions
sections.content:
A mobile ad hoc network (MANET) has wireless links that can change with movement and signal conditions. The network has no central controller, so nodes make routing and relaying decisions themselves.

Standard OSPF has no interface type that describes this wireless behavior. It can also send complete neighbor lists repeatedly, flood many routing updates, and form more adjacencies than a changing network needs. The RFC extends OSPFv3 to address these costs while supporting connections between MANET and wired networks.
sections.plainLanguage: In a MANET, the set of reachable neighbors can change over time. OSPF-OR changes how OSPF describes wireless links and shares routing information.

sections.title: The OSPF-MANET Interface
sections.content:
OSPF-OR represents a MANET interface using the point-to-multipoint model. OSPF treats router-to-router connections on it as point-to-point links, and a link metric can be set for each neighbor.

The interface can use Layer 2 broadcast, pseudo-broadcast, or no broadcast support. OSPF should use multicast packets; when the underlying link cannot provide multicast, OSPF must replicate them itself. A MANET interface does not require an IPv6 global unicast address.
sections.plainLanguage: The new interface type describes a wireless link where not every pair of nodes can communicate both ways. OSPF can still send multicast updates by copying them when the link requires it.

sections.title: Incremental Hello Messages
sections.content:
Normal OSPF Hello messages repeat the full neighbor list, even when it has not changed. Incremental Hellos send state changes instead. The I-bit marks this use, and the State Check Sequence (SCS) TLV carries a circular two-octet state number.

Other TLVs report dropped neighbors, request a neighbor's state, or identify a full-state response. If a receiver sees a missing sequence number, it requests current state because it may have missed an update. A full state is sent the first time a sequence number is used.
sections.plainLanguage: A Hello can report only the neighbor changes since the previous state. Its sequence number helps a receiver notice missing changes and ask for a full update.

sections.title: Overlapping Relays and Smart Peering
sections.content:
Overlapping relays reduce duplicate flooding. Each router learns its neighbors' neighbor lists, selects a set of relays that can reach its two-hop neighborhood, and signals that set in Hello messages. Selected relays should forward link-state advertisements promptly; other routers wait briefly and suppress transmissions that would be redundant.

Smart Peering can avoid forming an adjacency when the new neighbor is already reachable in the shortest-path tree. The decision is local, and implementations may use additional heuristics. The RFC warns that reducing links can increase the chance of suboptimal routes.
sections.plainLanguage: A selected subset of neighbors relays routing updates, while other nodes avoid sending copies that are no longer needed. A router can also skip a new adjacency when it already has a route to that neighbor.

sections.title: Security on Wireless Networks
sections.content:
The RFC says controlling which devices may join is outside its scope and points to link-layer security such as 802.1X. It also describes using the IPv6 Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload for authentication, integrity, and confidentiality.

These protections do not address compromised, malfunctioning, or misconfigured routers. The RFC says the OSPFv3 extensions introduce no new security threats, while noting that wireless links can make some attacks easier.
sections.plainLanguage: Wireless devices need separate controls for joining the network and for protecting routing messages. Those controls cannot make a compromised router trustworthy.
